title: Causal inference for multiple risk factors and diseases from genomics data.
paragraphs: Distinguishing causation from correlation is fundamentally important for understanding the etiology of common complex diseases. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard for causal inference, but their difficulty, expense, and ethical considerations often prohibit testing potential disease-associated risk factors across the vast array of human complex traits. As a result, the most commonly used methods for statistical causal inference in a genetic or biomedical setting center around the instrumental variable (IV) framework of Mendelian randomization (MR) 1 , 2 . A wide variety of MR approaches have been developed to test whether there exists a potential causal effect of one or more mediator variable(s) onto one or more outcome variable(s) using genome-wide association study (GWAS) data 3 – 16 .

MR relies on core assumptions that: (1) the genetic instrumental variables are associated with the exposure (the relevance assumption); (2) there are no measured or unmeasured confounding variables of the instrumental variable and the outcome Y (termed the independence assumption); and (3) all paths between the instrumental variable and the outcome go through the exposure (exclusion restriction or no horizontal pleiotropy assumption). These assumptions are notoriously difficult to verify directly in empirical applications, and violations of independence and exclusion restriction in particular can substantially inflate type I error, producing spurious claims of causation where none exists 17 .

Theoretical developments in statistical causal inference show that graphical modeling can be used to learn the underlying causal structure of hundreds of variables, whilst controlling for potential unobserved confounding within a single model 18 – 20 . As we describe below, combining graphical inference with standard MR methods has the potential to prioritize exposure-outcome pairs and to select instrumental variables in a principled manner by explicitly verifying MR assumptions. However, there are currently no algorithms capable of conducting this form of causal discovery at scale. Developing these approaches to accommodate highly correlated variables across diverse distributions and millions of highly correlated genetic markers, whilst allowing data to be combined across biobanks, would facilitate accurate, high-throughput screening of potential causal links between modifiable risk factors and disease outcomes.

Here, we propose an approach for conducting Causal Inference in Genome-Wide Association Studies (CI-GWAS) that can infer a single graph at scale describing the relationships among millions of genetic markers, tens of risk factors and multiple disease outcomes. We utilize the inferred graph for more principled detection of potential IVs, controlling for linkage disequilibrium (LD) genome-wide and providing better empirical checking of core MR assumptions, in particular the absence of horizontal pleiotropy and potential latent confounding of the marker outcome relationship. In simulations, we show that CI-GWAS selects appropriate IVs and that this improves upon the high false discovery rates of current MR approaches under violation of the INSIDE assumption (i.e., correlated pleiotropy / heritable confounding). Our approach can accommodate rare variants and rare disease outcomes by placing relationships on the liability scale to correct for differences in outcome prevalence. Applying CI-GWAS to summary statistic data of 8.4 M SNPs and 15 phenotypes requires only 20 minutes of wall-clock compute time on a standard GPU server. We find that few GWAS variants are suitable MR IVs, but that many previously reported paths among risk factors and outcomes 11 can be recovered within both univariate and multivariable methods. Further investigation reveals that within the UK Biobank, unmeasured latent confounding cannot be ruled out as a potential underlying explanation for the phenotypic relationships that we report. CI-GWAS can be applied to individual-level or summary-statistic data and provides a potential solution for facilitating robust one- or two-sample MR inference on large-scale genotype-phenotype data.

Here, we present CI-GWAS, an algorithm designed to learn a graphical model that describes the causal relationships among genetic and phenotypic variables. CI-GWAS constructs such a model in two steps: (1) by learning a skeleton, an undirected graph over the set of observed variables; (2) by directing the edges in the skeleton to obtain a partial ancestral graph (PAG), while taking into account potential confounding through latent variables. The inferred graph encodes which causal relations are compatible with the data's conditional independence structure. In the following, we show how the learned graph can be used in conjunction with an MR method to infer a set of potential causal relationships and their effects.

In the first step, the skeleton is learned by a modified version of the PC-stable algorithm 21 , in which the correlations between observed pairs of variables are tested for significance, conditional on sets of other observed variables (see Methods for a thorough explanation). All edges between pairs for which any test has determined the association to be insignificant are removed from the graph. Thus, for any adjacent pair of variables in the final skeleton, there exists a degree of correlation that cannot be explained away by conditioning on any subset of observed variables.

One very useful property of the learned skeleton is that it enables the identification of likely valid instrumental variables for MR. We explicitly define valid MR instruments in a finite sample as those that are associated with the exposure but not with the outcome after conditioning on the exposure. We can identify valid IVs based on the conditional independence tests conducted, which ensure that the common MR assumptions about instrumental variables hold. In particular, by inspecting the learned graph, one can verify the following assumptions: (1) that the genetic instrumental variables are associated with the exposure; (2) that there are no measured or unmeasured confounding variables of the instrumental variable and the outcome Y ; and (3) that all paths between the instrumental variable and the outcome go through the exposure. The conditions that must be met in the learned graph for these assumptions to hold are simple: for a given exposure trait X and an outcome trait Y , any marker G , found to be adjacent to X and not adjacent to Y and for which all paths to Y contain X , is a valid instrument to test the effect of X on Y , under the assumption that the learned skeleton is faithful to the underlying distribution.

These conditions ensure that the relevance assumption holds for ( G , X ), because G and X are adjacent only if there is a significant effect of G on X that cannot be explained away by conditioning on any other measured variables. The independence assumption also holds for ( G , Y ), because, if G and Y are affected by unobserved latent confounding, a dependency is induced and G and Y remain adjacent in the skeleton, since no conducted test can remove the dependency. If they are, on the other hand, affected by a common confounding variable that is measured and therefore in the graph, then there is a path from G to Y that does not contain X , namely through that confounding variable. The exclusion restriction also holds for ( G , Y ) by similar arguments: if G has a direct effect on Y , they are adjacent in the graph. If G has an effect on Y that is mediated by a third variable L , this path can be either read off the graph (if L is measured) or again appears as an adjacency of G and Y if L is latent.

However, this approach has limitations. In particular, there exist configurations of effects and effect sizes under which these rules will produce false positive and also false negative IVs in the presence of unmeasured confounding. First, it is possible that ( G , Y ) are not adjacent in the skeleton even if there is a path from G to Y that does not include X . This happens when there exist multiple paths from G to Y in the data-generating structure whose total effect sizes cancel each other out 22 , 23 . If not all relevant variables are measured, the latent paths will not be visible in the graph, and G will be marked as a valid IV, thereby making a false positive error. Second, in the presence of an unmeasured confounder U of X and Y , G and Y may stay adjacent in the skeleton due to collider bias, if the association through the path G → X ← U → Y is large enough in magnitude to be significant in the conditional independence test. Our rules will produce false-negative errors in this situation, removing potentially valid instruments. In summary, this shows that by inspecting the learned skeleton, one can select variables for which the above-stated MR assumptions hold, assuming no latent confounding. However, the selection may be flawed if not all relevant variables are measured. We investigate to what extent confounding impacts the performance of our algorithm in extensive simulation experiments below.

Our procedure to learn the skeleton is based on a GPU-accelerated version of the PC-stable algorithm 21 , 24 , which we additionally accelerated by iterative variable selection and by exploiting the LD-block structure of the genome. This enables us to construct a complete marker-trait graph, for millions of markers and tens of traits, despite the exponential run-time scaling in the number of variables of the PC algorithm. One challenge here is that the PC algorithm relies on partial correlations vanishing for (conditionally) independent variables, which generally holds for Gaussian variables? but not necessarily for binary or ordinal variables. We find that treating binary case-control outcomes like Gaussian variables can lead to largely elevated numbers of false positive findings, especially for independence tests between markers with very low minor allele frequencies and binary traits with very unbalanced numbers of cases and controls (Supplementary Fig. 1 ). As has been shown in previous work 25 , a heterologous correlation matrix with Pearson correlations between Gaussian, polyserial between Gaussian and ordinal and polychoric correlations between ordinal variables can be used to prevent this issue. This effectively places binary variables on the liability scale and has the additional advantage of allowing comparisons among traits at the same scale, accounting for differences in outcome prevalence. At the sample size, lowest minor allele frequency and lowest trait prevalence in the UK Biobank data used in this study, using polyserial correlations between markers and case-control traits is effective in controlling the numbers of false positives (Supplementary Fig. 1 ).

This first step of the algorithm can be combined with the second to prioritize exposure-outcome pairs, through selection of risk factors that are most likely to have a significant directed partial correlation with a particular outcome. The second step is based on the RFCI algorithm 20 , which attempts to direct the edges of the learned skeleton, testing for the presence of latent confounding. We introduce a novel way to obtain order-independent separation sets that offer a conservative way of orienting trait relationships, that is, to learn which phenotypes have evidence for a potential directed relationship with each outcome. We also incorporate prior knowledge that markers precede traits temporally, which dramatically reduces computation time. We denote our version of RFCI as sRFCI. For further details, see Methods.

Taken together, we improve upon previously proposed graphical methods that were limited to few hundreds 26 or thousands 27 of genetic variables or relied on the construction of separate graphs for trait-trait and marker-trait relationships with pre-selected genetic variants by GWAS 17 . Combining graphical inference with standard MR methods takes advantage of the principled instrumental variable selection and the identification of relevant risk factors. This also advances previous work on graphical inference in MR 17 because now marker selection is made through joint estimation, where many variables can be conditioned on at once, and pleiotropic markers can be identified prior to MR inference, promising more accurate instrumental variable selection and improved MR performance as shown below.

CI-GWAS takes as input: (1) the matrix of marker-marker correlations (an LD matrix); (2) a matrix of marker-trait correlations; (3) a matrix of trait-trait correlations. This makes CI-GWAS applicable to summary-statistic data, since LD matrices, effect sizes of marker-trait associations, minor allele frequencies, trait variances and trait-trait correlations can be shared whilst preserving privacy.

Here, we study how the usage of IVs selected by CI-GWAS in MR compares to standard GWAS-based IV selection. To this end, we conduct a simulation study using 654,173 imputed genetic markers recorded on 458,747 UK Biobank individuals (see Methods). We simulate data according to the graph generally considered in MR studies, shown in Fig. 1 a. We generate strong unobserved confounding, U , influencing both the exposure and outcome of interest, and focus on the three MR assumptions, given above, by simulating six scenarios where: (1) genetic effects are strong and therefore easily identifiable and there is no horizontal pleiotropy, or latent genetic confounding (labeled: baseline, high power); (2) genetic effects are weak and therefore more difficult to identify, effects are estimated with higher error and there is no horizontal pleiotropy or latent genetic confounding (labeled: baseline, low power); (3) genetic effects are easily identifiable and there is latent genetic confounding (latent pleiotropy, high power); (4) genetic effects are difficult to identify and there is latent genetic confounding (latent pleiotropy, low power); (5) genetic effects are easily identifiable and there is both latent genetic confounding and horizontal pleiotropy (horizontal pleiotropy, high power), which is also termed correlated pleiotropy or heritable confounding in the literature; (6) genetic effects are difficult to identify and there is both latent genetic confounding and horizontal pleiotropy (horizontal pleiotropy, low power). For each scenario, we simulate the exposure to be either causal for the outcome with average causal effect A C E = 0.2, or non-causal for the outcome A C E = 0.0, resulting in 12 settings for which we simulate 100 replicates. Thus, we generate 1200 data sets in total, each with a sample size of 458,747 individuals and a feature size of 654,172 SNPs.

For each of these data sets, we select IVs in two ways. First, we run standard marginal linear regression for X and Y at each of the 654,172 SNPs and then select IVs as an independent set of SNPs (within 1Mb, with LD R 2 < 0.001) associated with X with p value ≤5 × 10 −8 , as is commonly done in MR studies. Second, we use CI-GWAS to select the IVs as described above: For a given exposure trait X and an outcome trait Y , any marker G , found to be adjacent to X and not adjacent to Y and for which all paths to Y contain X , is discovered as a valid instrument to test the effect of X on Y . We then use these IVs alongside their marginal GWAS regression coefficients in two commonly used MR approaches of inverse-variance weighting (IVW) and MR-Egger 12 to estimate the causal effect of the exposure X and outcome Y .

We find that selecting genetic IVs from CI-GWAS allows unbiased estimation of the ACE across all scenarios considered here, when using both IVW and MR-Egger, as shown Fig. 1b . This accurate ACE estimation is further reflected in the false positive rate (FPR) of zero for each of the twelve settings (Fig. 1c ). In contrast to that, we see a considerable effect of horizontal pleiotropy for both MR-methods used with GWAS selected IVs. Note here, FPR measures the proportion of simulation replicates where A C E = 0, but MR methods incorrectly identify a causal effect of the exposure X and outcome Y (at p -value ≤0.05/800), out of all actual negatives (100 replicates per setting where A C E = 0). While MR-Egger shows zero FPR and little bias in the baseline setting, this changes to clear bias and a FPR of 0.6 and close to 1 in the presence of horizontal pleiotropy. Similarly, bias and FPR increase markedly for IVW in that setting. This suggests that the usage of IVs selected by CI-GWAS can help to avoid biases and false positives in MR inference that are introduced through either latent or horizontal pleiotropy.

We then compare the IVs detected by CI-GWAS to those identified by the standard approach from GWAS summary statistics (associated with X with p -value ≤5 × 10 −8 with LD R 2 < 0.001 within 1Mb). True valid IVs are those that are simulated to be associated with X , but not pleiotropic with Y or U . We find that CI-GWAS has a true positive rate (TPR, defined as the proportion of IVs correctly identified) comparable to GWAS for the selection of valid IVs under the horizontal pleiotropy settings considered here, but with a slight loss of power (Fig. 1d ). Additionally, we calculate the proportion of selected IVs for X that are also causal for Y through a path that is not through X or pleiotropic with Y (labeled PHP: proportion of horizontally pleiotropic IVs in Fig. 1d ). We find that CI-GWAS selected IVs are less likely to be causal for Y through a path that is not through X or pleiotropic with Y than IVs selected through GWAS, which explains why CI-GWAS improves causal effect estimates under both latent and horizontal pleiotropy.

As mentioned above, the graphical model learned by CI-GWAS indicates which potential causal relationships are compatible with the data's conditional independence structure. Consequently, one can use it to filter out hypothetical causal relationships that are not compatible with that conditional independence structure, with the aim of reducing the number of false positive results and exploring the nature of the trait relationships. Here, we explore two ways of doing that: (1) we inspect the skeleton and filter for pairs of variables that are adjacent. While non-adjacent pairs of variables may generally be in a causal relationship with each other, that relationship is mediated at least by one other observed variable, and the effect is therefore not direct. (2) We inspect the PAG and filter for pairs between which there is a directed or semi-directed edge, as for these, the conditional independence structure of the data does not provide any evidence against the existence of a causal effect (see Methods for more details).

We conduct an additional simulation experiment to investigate the effect of these filters. For that, we repeat the data generation for the four horizontal pleiotropy scenarios described above (high/low power and ACE=0.0/ACE=0.2 for X 1 to Y ), but modified the graph to include an additional exposure variable ( X 2), which does not have a causal effect on Y (ACE=0.0 for X 2 to Y , see Fig. 2 a and Methods). Thus, here, true causal relationships exist only from X 1 onto Y , and horizontal pleiotropy occurs either through unmeasured variables or through X 2. To perform the MR tests, we use IVW and multivariable inverse-variance weighting (MVIVW). We then assess the performance with and without the above described filtering strategies, which yields three distinct scenarios: MR tests are run on all exposure-outcome pairs (labeled s1 in Fig. 2 ); MR tests are run only on exposure-outcome pairs that are adjacent in the skeleton (labeled s2); and lastly, MR tests are run only on exposure outcome pairs for which there is either a directed or semi-directed edge from exposure to outcome in the PAG (labeled s3). For edges that were filtered out, we set the inferred A C E = 0 for the calculation of the performance metrics. We then calculate the FPR, TPR and true discovery rate (TDR) of the inferred causal relationships, where we calculate the rates as proportions of simulation replicates, since in each replicate, there is at most one causal link between an exposure and the outcome. For example, the FPR measures the proportion of simulation replicates where the true A C E = 0, but we incorrectly identify a causal effect of one of the exposures, X 1 or X 2, on the outcome Y . We find that the proposed filters are effective in reducing the FPR when using GWAS-selected IVs, but have only a little room left to reduce the FPR when using CI-GWAS selected IVs (Fig. 2b ), since that in itself brings the FPR down to almost 0, as already shown above (Fig. 1c ). Analyzing the effect on the TPR (Fig. 2b ), we see that the filters are not perfectly specific to false positives, but remove true positives as well, showing a classical recall-precision tradeoff, which is already evident when focusing only on the effect of GWAS vs CI-GWAS selected markers (s1). This is because, particularly in low-powered settings, the causal relationship between X1 and Y cannot always be directed due to simulated unobserved confounding and horizontal pleiotropy. Looking at the TDR, i.e., the proportion of identified causal effects that are actually true, we see that CI-GWAS-selected IVs yield extremely precise results across all settings with TDRs at or above 0.85. When looking only at relationships that can be directed, the TDR is further improved with the filters up to a TDR close to 1, even in the low power scenario. When using GWAS-selected IVs, we see that the PAG filter (s3) can bring a strong TDR improvement of about 0.2. The effects of the filters on the performance are consistent across IVW and MVIVW, with MVIVW generally yielding higher TDR at similar TPR, compared to IVW. Overall, we see that by trading recall for precision, CI-GWAS provides ways to refine causal inference in these simulation settings.

In the settings above, we have explored CI-GWAS in a very classical setting where it is pre-determined which traits are potential exposures and which are outcomes. Here, we move to a more complex scenario where we have a set of traits of interests and make no such assumptions about the causal structure, but instead allow that every trait might be causal for any other trait. Starting there, our aim is to infer the structure of the causal graph that relates these traits.

To study how well such a task can be solved by using CI-GWAS in conjunction with MR, we create an expanded simulation study in which we simulate many correlated traits and multiple latent confounders. We use a structural equation model consisting of twelve continuous traits, two of which are latent confounders and are not used in the inference. Each trait is influenced by a set of 50 causal markers randomly selected from 654,173 imputed genetic markers recorded for 458,747 UK Biobank individuals. Here, we include two additional MR approaches in the comparison, namely CAUSE 11 and MV-PRESSO 8 , in addition to MVIVW. We compare their performance when used with GWAS IV selection (MR ( I V G )) as input, and in conjunction with CI-GWAS IVs (MR ( I V C I G )). We then repeat the analyses using the CI-GWAS filters of the learned adjacencies (+ adj: using all adjacent pairs in the skeleton) or the PAG (using all pairs with evidence of a directed relationship). Since we assume that there are no pre-determined exposures and outcomes, we run CAUSE, which is a single-outcome, single-exposure model, for each simulated trait pair. For the multivariable approaches, we test each trait as an outcome, with all other traits treated as risk factors. When using the CI-GWAS inferred graph as a filter: we only conduct MR testing with CAUSE for trait pairs that have an adjacency, or a corresponding directed edge in the PAG; while for the multivariable approaches, we only select traits to include as exposures that have an adjacency, or a corresponding directed edge in the PAG. We simulate only a well-powered setting with a limited degree of horizontal pleiotropy as this allows us to compare approaches in an idealistic setting, where the results are not obscured by the lack of implicit control for horizontal pleiotropy of GWAS IV selection (see Methods). We run 20 replicates as this number was sufficient to support the conclusions of the simulations that we have already presented above.

We make the following observations: First, as shown above in Fig. 2 , filtering standard MR results with the CI-GWAS-learned adjacencies increases the TDR for all three tested MR methods (MR ( I V G ) vs. MR ( I V G ) + adj in Fig. 3 ). Second, the TDR is further increased, at the expense of power (TPR), by using the PAG instead of the skeleton for filtering (MR ( I V G ) + adj vs. MR ( I V G ) + PAG in Fig. 3 ). Third, for methods such as MV-PRESSO and MVIVW, only by using the PAG for filtering is an FDR of 0.05 achieved at a p -value threshold of 0.05 for the testing of the average causal effect (Fig. 3b ). Fourth, as CAUSE conducts variable selection on the marginal GWAS associations to select IVs, we find no evidence for improved performance when restricting CAUSE to using only CI-GWAS selected IVs. However, inference is more precise, with higher power when using the CI-GWAS-learned adjacencies. Finally, MVIVW with the PAG learned by CI-GWAS and CI-GWAS-selected IVs has a comparable FDR of 0.05 to CAUSE, but has significantly improved TPR. We find that these results remain largely consistent with different selection thresholds for GWAS (p-value ≤10 −4 ), when more markers are selected (Supplementary Figs. 2, 3, 5 ) and when pleiotropic effects are removed from the simulation (Supplementary Figs. 3, 5 ). Thus, we show that learning a graphical model, as in CI-GWAS, can be used in conjunction with traditional MR methods to improve precision. We apply CI-GWAS to 15 traits and 8.4 million single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers in UK Biobank data, as described in the Methods and Supplementary Table 1 . To compare our results to previous findings, we first analyze 36 pairs of risk factors and outcomes (single r.f.), focusing on four outcomes: asthma (AT), cardiovascular disease (CAD), stroke (ST), and type-2 diabetes (T2D). We then analyze all risk factors jointly with each outcome within an MVIVW framework (joint r.f).

Analyses, we find overall 1052 unique markers, which decline to 696 in the joint r.f. analyses that are suitable IVs. We find that the composition of the SNP sets varies between the single r.f. and the joint r.f. analyses (Supplementary Fig. 6 ), as expected due to the varying correlation between the traits considered. In the right panel of Fig. 4 , we compare our single r.f. results to those obtained by CAUSE in the UK Biobank presented in ref. 11 . IVW with CI-GWAS adjacencies and CI-GWAS identified IVs (CI-GWAS single r.f.) recover all of the suggested statistically causal paths found by CAUSE, with the exception of height (HT) to CAD and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) to ST. In addition to those discovered by CAUSE, we find paths from blood glucose levels (GLU) to both CAD and ST, from triglycerides (TRIG) to CAD and T2D, from low-density lipoproteins (LDL) to stroke (ST) and waist-hip ratio (WHR) to CAD (Fig. 4c ). This supports our simulation results, which showed that our algorithm performs similarly to CAUSE, with moderately improved power.

We then move from pair-wise single r.f. testing to using MVIVW with CI-GWAS adjacencies and CI-GWAS identified IVs (CI-GWAS joint r.f.), again focusing on the four outcomes of AT, CAD, ST and T2D as the outcome variables in MVIVW. Here, CI-GWAS joint r.f. finds GLU and WHR as potential causal risk factors for both CAD and T2D. HDL and LDL are also potential causal risk factors for CAD, and we find that LDL remains a potential causal risk factor for ST.

We then filter the exposure-outcome relationships more conservatively using the inferred directed edges in the PAG. We find that only the relationship between GLU and CAD persists (Supplementary Fig. 7 ). In addition, we find a directed edge from HDL onto AT, for which there is support in neither the previous CAUSE nor in our MVIVW results (Supplementary Fig. 7 ), but support in the literature 28 . All other previous potential causal relationships that are significant in CAUSE, the CI-GWAS single r.f. and the CI-GWAS joint r.f. analyses, are assigned a bi-directed edge in the inferred PAG returned by part 2 of our algorithm. Here, a bi-directed edge is defined as two observed variables that directly influence each other simultaneously (a feedback loop or mutual causation occurring too quickly to observe directionality in the data), or are governed by unobserved selection variables, reflecting the presence of a latent confounder. Thus, within the UK Biobank, our model suggests that all of the other potential causal relationships inferred (e.g., by CAUSE presented in ref. 11 ) may be explained by feedback loops, mutual causation, or unmeasured latent confounding. Latent confounding may reflect processes like population structure, study ascertainment, linkage, shared parental effects, shared environment and/or assortative mating.

Here, we present a method for statistical causal inference in a genomic setting to learn a graph by inferring the adjacencies from partial correlations, orienting the edges and then estimating the strength of the causal effects, whilst allowing for the presence of multiple confounders and multiple correlated phenotypes. The algorithms we present have strong theoretical support and have been heavily studied in the causal inference literature 20 , 21 , 29 . We demonstrate that extending statistical causal discovery from MR methods to multivariable graphical inference for large GWAS or biobank data sets with millions of variables and hundreds of thousands of records provides: (1) appropriate selection of IVs that are likely to fulfill MR assumptions, and (2) robust inference of potential causal links with greatly reduced false discovery rates and fast run time for both continuous and binary measurements. Current MR methods generally give consistent results, they all build upon each other, assume a similar fixed directed acyclic graph and can have high type-I error. Here, we show empirical evidence for this and how this can be addressed by combining existing MR approaches with graphical inference.

High-dimensional non-sparse graphical causal inference is an active area of research, and there have been a number of proposed alternatives to the approach presented here, such as various alternative forms of multivariable MR 8 , 30 , 31 . Here, we show that MR is ineffective without being paired with graphical inference. Structural equation models have also been suggested 32 , but these require a correct causal order of variables to be known (or learned) and are cumbersome to run on large-scale high-dimensional data, even in summary statistic form. A number of artificial intelligence approaches have recently been presented for causal inference in life science settings 33 . However, these lack rigorous theory and an understanding of the conditions required for these algorithms to recover meaningful causal structures and estimates. As a result, while estimates are obtained, one has little assurance that reliable inference is obtained, much like standard MR approaches. Thus, we focus here on applying and developing a principled, theoretically supported method that provides a crucial step toward high-dimensional statistical causal learning for genomics.

A number of limitations remain. Our approach requires either individual-level data or summary information on the minor allele frequency, the LD correlations, and the phenotypic correlations, alongside standard GWAS regression coefficient estimates. This level of summary data is not always publicly available, but could easily be shared, inferred across biobanks, or approximated. Data sets have a structure that can inhibit unbiased causal inference, such as selection biases like the ascertainment of healthy older people into biobank studies, which can bias causal inference 34 . Additionally, there is also a general tendency in the UK Biobank sampled individuals for almost everyone to be under some form of medical intervention. In particular, natural variation in lipid levels and blood pressure may be impossible to observe within the UK Biobank as the majority of people are being treated with some form of drug. Here, we adjust for the effects of drug taking prior to analysis, but if the majority have interventions, this is likely ineffective, and a larger-scale model investigating prescriptions, observations and outcomes through repeated measures may be more effective. By utilizing longitudinal records, where discovered adjacencies in the skeleton can then be orientated longitudinally and combined with therapeutic information, statistical causal effects may be more effectively examined as there is certainty about the directions of many time ordered edges. This will then reduce the number of bi-directed edges learned in the PAG. Our approach easily facilitates this and we are actively working on this topic. Finally, genotype-phenotype associations likely reflect a complex combination of direct, parental genetic and epigenetic effects, and this may also be why we infer a large number of relationships to occur due to latent confounding. Parental genotypes and their relationship to offspring traits could also be accommodated within our framework, but at this time there is a lack of large-scale family data.

In summary, our approach is applicable to screen for potential causal relationships within life-science data, from genomics to the microbiome to single-cell sequencing and phenotyping datasets. This may be very fruitful as trait-omics associations are often stronger than marker-trait correlations, giving improved recall rates. By combining methods of genetic epidemiology and statistical causal inference, within algorithms that require only summary statistic correlations from the data, we expect that our work will facilitate extensive investigation of potential causal hypotheses. We show that inferring causal relationships from simple observational biobank data is limited, and our results call for caution when applying current MR methods to biobank data. With any dataset, we feel that it is important to understand which relationships hold under which assumptions, and our approach provides a way to screen associations under explicit checks. This way, more can be learned about the likely underlying nature of phenotypic and genetic correlations within the human population.

CI-GWAS takes either individual or summary-level data, learns conditional dependencies between genetic variants and traits and determines whether conditional dependencies among traits can be attributed to a directed causal relationship. It can then estimate, in conjunction with a Mendelian Randomization method, the magnitude and direction of the potential causal effect. A full analysis with CI-GWAS consists of three computational steps: (1) a GPU-accelerated algorithm that conducts genetic variable selection and returns an undirected graph that describes the potential causal relationships among markers and traits (called cuda-skeleton); (2) an approach called sRFCI that directs the skeleton edges and thereby infers causal relationships, allowing for arbitrarily many latent variables; and (3) estimation of the magnitude of the potential causal relationships among the discovered exposures and outcomes with a MR method like multi-variable inverse weighted Mendelian Randomization (MVIVW) 9 . This final part uses the sets of directly associated markers for each trait as instrument variables, which conform to the assumptions of MVIVW. Additionally, we propose only estimating exposure-outcome effects for trait-trait conditional dependencies discovered by either cuda-skeleton or sRFCI that are also significant in MVIVW. We provide detailed information on each step of CI-GWAS in the following sections, along with algorithms for their implementation.

Having inferred a skeleton, we propose to infer the direction of causal relationships by orienting the graph edges. For this, we employ two procedures: (1) inference of a partial ancestral graph (PAG) by a modified RFCI 20 algorithm (sRFCI); and (2) multi-variable inverse variance weighted Mendelian randomization (MVIVW) 9 , or a comparable method, as described in the following section.

Unobserved confounding variables (i.e., latent variables) are a common problem for the inference of causal relationships. They indicate violation of causal sufficiency (i.e., knowledge of all causally important variables in the graph), which is a common assumption in causal inference. In consequence, a variable may be inferred as causal for another even though there is no causal relationship between the two. To allow for an additional check for unobserved variables, we devise an approach based on the RFCI algorithm 20 for the inference of causal graphs, which allows for arbitrarily many latent variables in the true underlying directed acyclic graph (DAG). True separation sets, i.e., the full set of variables that render two non-adjacent variables independent when conditioned upon, are difficult to obtain when marker-trait effects are weak. We observed that weak marker-trait effects result in incomplete separation sets, causing traits to be missing from the separation sets of markers and other traits, thereby giving incorrect edge orientation. To solve this issue, we present an order-independent algorithm that uses the RFCI procedure to orient edges between adjacent variables, whilst considering a locally maximal number of variables in the separation sets used to infer the orientations. Specifically, we infer two types of separation sets: (1) S m a x , a maximal separation set, meaning that the addition of any other variable results in Z > τ , and (2) S m p c a subset of the maximal separation set that locally minimizes the partial correlation between variables V i and V j .

S m a x is conservative as to what is not included in the separation set. Thus, everything that is not within S m a x can be considered a collider between the variables. This separation set is used within sRFCI to orient unshielded triples, as described below. A triple of nodes V i , V k and V j is unshielded if all of the following are true: (1) V i and V k are connected; (2) V k and V j are connected; (3) V i and V j are not connected. The output of this algorithm is a Partial Ancestral Graph (PAG) representing a set of possible Maximal Ancestral Graphs (MAG, see ref. 20 for definition). Adjacencies are inferred to be composed of arrows ( < or > ), circles (∘), and tails ( − ). An arrow at a variable implies that the variable is not ancestral to the variable at the other end of the edge. The tail implies that the variable is ancestral to the variable at the other end of the edge. Circles represent arrowheads in some MAGs in the Markov equivalence class represented by the PAG and tails in others. RFCI allows inference of causal information in the presence of latent variables and hidden factors or confounders 20 , which has been shown to be of importance for Mendelian Randomization methods applied to biobank data 6 , 11 , 42 – 44 . A situation can arise when neither variable is ancestral to the other, which results in the adjacency being inferred as ↔ . This implies that neither variable is ancestral to the other, with no direct causal relationship inferred, suggesting the existence of a latent confounder. Numerically, the algorithm outputs: 0 = no edge; 1 = circle; 2 = tail; 3 = arrow. Throughout this work, we use the following interpretation, circle-circle: undirected edge, uncertain orientation; circle-arrow: partial edge, potential causal link; tail-arrow: directed edge, unambiguous potential causal link; arrow-arrow: bidirected edge, indicating hidden latent confounding; circle-tail: semi-directed edge, potential causal link; tail-tail: undirected edge, insufficient data available. To select a set of relationships with clear causal direction from the output of this procedure, we select all inferred edges with one arrow and one tail, since these are invariant across the MAGs represented by the PAG and therefore are inferred to have a definite orientation. We note that a PAG represents a set of graphs that all share certain structures (i.e., node adjacency causal relations), and it is possible that the information on conditional independence in the data is insufficient to uniquely determine the exact type of an edge. Thus, it is also possible to relax the selection to relationships that include both directed and semi-directed edges, as for these, the conditional independence structure of the data does not provide any evidence against the existence of such an effect.

Having learned the conditional dependencies in the data with cuda-skeleton and tested for latent confounding among traits with sRFCI, we propose using the MVIVW framework, or a comparable method, to assess the significance and magnitude of causal effects.

To identify potential causal relationships in an MR framework, such as MVIVW, sets of IVs and exposures are needed for each outcome. Specifically, MVIVW assumes that IVs associated with at least one exposure are not associated with any latent confounders of the exposures and outcome, and are conditionally independent of the outcome given the exposures, i.e., that all causal paths from the IV to the outcome go through the exposures, and that there is no latent confounder of IV and outcome 9 , 45 . MVIVW can be employed using the SNPs inferred from cuda-skeleton because the conditional-independence tests conducted in cuda-skeleton explicitly check for several common MR assumptions on IVs (see ref. 45 for a discussion of those assumptions). In consequence, valid IVs can be directly read off the skeleton. In particular, for a given exposure trait A and an outcome trait B , any marker X adjacent to A that is not adjacent to B is a valid instrument to test the effect of A on B (assuming the skeleton is faithful to the underlying distribution) for the following reasons: If X had a direct effect on B , the dependency should not have been removed by any conducted test. Thus, the exclusion restriction holds. If marker X and the outcome B relationship was confounded by a latent variable, that confounding would induce a dependency, and again, X and B should remain adjacent in the skeleton, since no conducted test should be able to remove the dependency. Thus, the effect of X on B should not be confounded.

If marker X and the outcome B relationship was confounded by a latent variable, that confounding would induce a dependency, and again, X and B should remain adjacent in the skeleton, since no conducted test should be able to remove the dependency. Thus, the effect of X on B should not be confounded.

Note that the above only holds as long as all traits in the model, except for the outcome, are used as exposures in a multivariable MR analysis. This is necessary because X could also be associated with B through the omitted trait, which could either have in turn an effect on B and thereby invalidate the exclusion restriction. Thus, for single-variable MR like IVW, IV candidates need to be further verified by checking that the inferred graphical model does not contain a path from the IV to the outcome that does not include the exposure.

Principled instrumental selection of this kind contrasts with most other current MR approaches, in which IVs are selected by selecting variants with the highest marginal association test statistics. A similar approach, based on the association of markers with a single trait, while having multiple traits in the model, has been proven to be valid and successfully applied in previous work 17 . Here, we advance this idea within a framework in which no markers need to be pre-selected, many variables can be conditioned on simultaneously, and pleiotropic markers can be used for inference, thereby promising more accurate IV selection and powerful analysis.

For each outcome, we assess the significance and estimate the effect size of each potential exposure using MVIVW with unfiltered parental markers (conforming to the criteria above) as instrumental variables. We use all traits in the model, aside from the outcome, as exposures. From here, we select only the links that are selected as significant in cuda-skeleton or are directed in the same way as inferred by MVIVW in the sRFCI inferred PAG. This provides sets of potential causal links with evidence of directionality learned from the data.

UK Biobank has approval from the North-West Multicenter Research Ethics Committee (MREC) to obtain and disseminate data and samples from the participants ( https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ethics/ ). These ethical regulations cover the work in this study. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. From the measurements, tests, and electronic health record data available in the UK Biobank data 47 , we selected six blood-based biomarkers, four of the most common heritable complex diseases, and seven quantitative measures. The full list of the 15 traits, the UK Biobank coding of the data used, and the covariates adjusted for are given in Supplementary Table 1 . For the quantitative measures and blood-based biomarkers, we adjusted the values by the covariates, removed any individuals with a phenotype greater or less than 7 SD from the mean (assuming these are measurement errors), and standardized the values to have a mean of 0 and a variance of 1.

For the common complex diseases, we determined disease status using a combination of available information. For asthma (AT), we used self-reported asthma diagnosis by a doctor (3786-0.0), date of asthma report (42014-0.0), and self-reported recent asthma medication (22167-0.0). For cardiovascular disease (CAD), we used self-report information of whether a heart attack was diagnosed by a doctor (3894-0.0), the age angina was diagnosed (3627-0.0), whether the individual reported a heart problem diagnosed by a doctor (6150-0.0), and the date of myocardial infarction (42,000-0.0). For stroke (ST), we used self-report stroke diagnosed by a doctor (6150-0.0), the age at which stroke was diagnosed (4056-0.0). For type-2 diabetes (T2D), we used self-report information of whether diabetes was diagnosed by a doctor (2443-0.0), the age diabetes was diagnosed (2976-0.0), and whether the individual reported taking diabetes medication (6153-0.0, 6177-0.0). For each disease, we then combined this with primary death ICD10 codes (40001-0.0), causes of operative procedures (41201-0.0), and the main (41202-0.0), secondary (41204-0.0) and inpatient ICD10 codes (41270-0.0). For AT, we selected all ICD10 J45 codes, for CAD we selected ICD10 codes I20-I29, for ST we selected all ICD10 I6 codes, and for T2D we selected ICD10 codes E11 to E14 and excluded from the analysis individuals with E10 (type-1 diabetes). Thus, for the purposes of this analysis, we define these diseases broadly simply to maximize the number of cases available for analysis. Individuals with neither a self-report indication nor a relevant ICD10 diagnosis were assigned a zero value as a control.

We first restricted our analysis to a sample of UK Biobank individuals of European ancestry. To infer ancestry, we used both self-reported ethnic background (UK Biobank field 21000-0), selecting coding 1, and genetic ethnicity (UK Biobank field 22006-0), selecting coding 1. We projected the 488,377 genotyped participants onto the first two genotypic principal components (PC) calculated from 2504 individuals of the 1000 Genomes project. Using the obtained PC loadings, we then assigned each participant to the closest 1000 Genomes project population, selecting individuals with PC1 projection ≤ absolute value 4 and PC2 projection ≤ absolute value 3. We applied this ancestry restriction to provide the first application of our approach and to replicate our results in a sample as genetically homogeneous as possible. Note, however, that our approach can be applied within different human groups (by age, genetic sex, ethnicity, etc.). Our future work will focus on exploring differences in causal inference across a diverse range of human populations.

Samples were also excluded based on UK Biobank quality control procedures with individuals removed of (1) extreme heterozygosity and missing genotype outliers; (2) a genetically inferred gender that did not match the self-reported gender; (3) putative sex chromosome aneuploidy; (4) exclusion from kinship inference; (5) withdrawn consent. We used genotype probabilities from version 3 of the imputed autosomal genotype data provided by the UK Biobank to hard-call the single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotypes for variants with an imputation quality score above 0.3. The hard-call threshold was 0.1, setting genotypes with probability ≤ 0.9 as missing. From the good quality markers (with missingness less than 5% and p -value for Hardy-Weinberg test larger than 10 −6 , as determined in the set of unrelated Europeans), we selected those with minor allele frequency (MAF) ≥0.0002 and rs identifier, in the set of European-ancestry participants. This resulted in a dataset with 458,747 individuals and 8,430,446 markers. We apply CI-GWAS to these data as described above and we use these data for our simulation study as described below.

To compare the causal inference performance, we calculate the false positive rate, FPR = false positives / (false positives + true negatives), for each MR approach for each of the settings. FPR measures the proportion of simulation replicates where A C E = 0, but MR methods incorrectly identify a causal effect of the exposure X and outcome Y (at p -value ≤0.05/800), out of all actual negatives (100 replicates per setting where A C E = 0). For the horizontal pleiotropy settings, the true positive rate (power), TPR = true positives / total positives, is calculated for the identified IVs, giving the proportion of IVs correctly identified by CI-GWAS, or standard GWAS across settings. We also calculate the proportion of selected IV SNPs for X that are also causal for Y through a path that is not through X (labeled PHP: proportion of horizontally pleiotropic IVs).

In the settings with two mediator variables, we calculate the false positive rate, FPR = false positives / (false positives + true negatives), of two commonly used MR approaches of inverse-variance weighting (IVW) and multivariable inverse-variance weighting (MVIVW). FPR measures the proportion of simulation replicates where A C E = 0, but MR methods incorrectly identify a causal effect of one of the exposures X 1 or X 2 and the outcome Y (at p -value ≤0.05/800), out of all actual negatives (600 occurrences in total, comprised of all of the 400 simulation replicates where A C E = 0 for X 2 to Y , and the 200 replicates where A C E = 0 for X 1 to Y ). We also compare the TPR (power), TPR = true positives / total positives, the proportion of causal relationships correctly identified by CI-GWAS, or standard GWAS, across settings. We give the true discovery rate, TDR = true positives / total discoveries, the proportion of identified causal relationships by CI-GWAS, or standard GWAS, that are true across settings. First, TPR and TDR are calculated for all tested relationships. We then calculate TPR and TDR, setting all non-adjacent edges in the graph to A C E = 0.0, as the undirected graph does not find a causal relationship. Finally, FPR, TPR and TDR are calculated after all edges in the partial ancestral graph (PAG) for which no potential directed relationship is found are set to A C E = 0.0.

Distinguishing causation from correlation is fundamentally important for understanding the etiology of common complex diseases. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard for causal inference, but their difficulty, expense, and ethical considerations often prohibit testing potential disease-associated risk factors across the vast array of human complex traits. As a result, the most commonly used methods for statistical causal inference in a genetic or biomedical setting center around the instrumental variable (IV) framework of Mendelian randomization (MR) 1 , 2 . A wide variety of MR approaches have been developed to test whether there exists a potential causal effect of one or more mediator variable(s) onto one or more outcome variable(s) using genome-wide association study (GWAS) data 3 – 16 .

MR relies on core assumptions that: (1) the genetic instrumental variables are associated with the exposure (the relevance assumption); (2) there are no measured or unmeasured confounding variables of the instrumental variable and the outcome Y (termed the independence assumption); and (3) all paths between the instrumental variable and the outcome go through the exposure (exclusion restriction or no horizontal pleiotropy assumption). These assumptions are notoriously difficult to verify directly in empirical applications, and violations of independence and exclusion restriction in particular can substantially inflate type I error, producing spurious claims of causation where none exists 17 .

Theoretical developments in statistical causal inference show that graphical modeling can be used to learn the underlying causal structure of hundreds of variables, whilst controlling for potential unobserved confounding within a single model 18 – 20 . As we describe below, combining graphical inference with standard MR methods has the potential to prioritize exposure-outcome pairs and to select instrumental variables in a principled manner by explicitly verifying MR assumptions. However, there are currently no algorithms capable of conducting this form of causal discovery at scale. Developing these approaches to accommodate highly correlated variables across diverse distributions and millions of highly correlated genetic markers, whilst allowing data to be combined across biobanks, would facilitate accurate, high-throughput screening of potential causal links between modifiable risk factors and disease outcomes.

Here, we propose an approach for conducting Causal Inference in Genome-Wide Association Studies (CI-GWAS) that can infer a single graph at scale describing the relationships among millions of genetic markers, tens of risk factors and multiple disease outcomes. We utilize the inferred graph for more principled detection of potential IVs, controlling for linkage disequilibrium (LD) genome-wide and providing better empirical checking of core MR assumptions, in particular the absence of horizontal pleiotropy and potential latent confounding of the marker outcome relationship. In simulations, we show that CI-GWAS selects appropriate IVs and that this improves upon the high false discovery rates of current MR approaches under violation of the INSIDE assumption (i.e., correlated pleiotropy / heritable confounding). Our approach can accommodate rare variants and rare disease outcomes by placing relationships on the liability scale to correct for differences in outcome prevalence. Applying CI-GWAS to summary statistic data of 8.4 M SNPs and 15 phenotypes requires only 20 minutes of wall-clock compute time on a standard GPU server. We find that few GWAS variants are suitable MR IVs, but that many previously reported paths among risk factors and outcomes 11 can be recovered within both univariate and multivariable methods. Further investigation reveals that within the UK Biobank, unmeasured latent confounding cannot be ruled out as a potential underlying explanation for the phenotypic relationships that we report. CI-GWAS can be applied to individual-level or summary-statistic data and provides a potential solution for facilitating robust one- or two-sample MR inference on large-scale genotype-phenotype data.

Here, we present CI-GWAS, an algorithm designed to learn a graphical model that describes the causal relationships among genetic and phenotypic variables. CI-GWAS constructs such a model in two steps: (1) by learning a skeleton, an undirected graph over the set of observed variables; (2) by directing the edges in the skeleton to obtain a partial ancestral graph (PAG), while taking into account potential confounding through latent variables. The inferred graph encodes which causal relations are compatible with the data's conditional independence structure. In the following, we show how the learned graph can be used in conjunction with an MR method to infer a set of potential causal relationships and their effects.

In the first step, the skeleton is learned by a modified version of the PC-stable algorithm 21 , in which the correlations between observed pairs of variables are tested for significance, conditional on sets of other observed variables (see Methods for a thorough explanation). All edges between pairs for which any test has determined the association to be insignificant are removed from the graph. Thus, for any adjacent pair of variables in the final skeleton, there exists a degree of correlation that cannot be explained away by conditioning on any subset of observed variables.

One very useful property of the learned skeleton is that it enables the identification of likely valid instrumental variables for MR. We explicitly define valid MR instruments in a finite sample as those that are associated with the exposure but not with the outcome after conditioning on the exposure. We can identify valid IVs based on the conditional independence tests conducted, which ensure that the common MR assumptions about instrumental variables hold. In particular, by inspecting the learned graph, one can verify the following assumptions: (1) that the genetic instrumental variables are associated with the exposure; (2) that there are no measured or unmeasured confounding variables of the instrumental variable and the outcome Y ; and (3) that all paths between the instrumental variable and the outcome go through the exposure. The conditions that must be met in the learned graph for these assumptions to hold are simple: for a given exposure trait X and an outcome trait Y , any marker G , found to be adjacent to X and not adjacent to Y and for which all paths to Y contain X , is a valid instrument to test the effect of X on Y , under the assumption that the learned skeleton is faithful to the underlying distribution.

These conditions ensure that the relevance assumption holds for ( G , X ), because G and X are adjacent only if there is a significant effect of G on X that cannot be explained away by conditioning on any other measured variables. The independence assumption also holds for ( G , Y ), because, if G and Y are affected by unobserved latent confounding, a dependency is induced and G and Y remain adjacent in the skeleton, since no conducted test can remove the dependency. If they are, on the other hand, affected by a common confounding variable that is measured and therefore in the graph, then there is a path from G to Y that does not contain X , namely through that confounding variable. The exclusion restriction also holds for ( G , Y ) by similar arguments: if G has a direct effect on Y , they are adjacent in the graph. If G has an effect on Y that is mediated by a third variable L , this path can be either read off the graph (if L is measured) or again appears as an adjacency of G and Y if L is latent.

However, this approach has limitations. In particular, there exist configurations of effects and effect sizes under which these rules will produce false positive and also false negative IVs in the presence of unmeasured confounding. First, it is possible that ( G , Y ) are not adjacent in the skeleton even if there is a path from G to Y that does not include X . This happens when there exist multiple paths from G to Y in the data-generating structure whose total effect sizes cancel each other out 22 , 23 . If not all relevant variables are measured, the latent paths will not be visible in the graph, and G will be marked as a valid IV, thereby making a false positive error. Second, in the presence of an unmeasured confounder U of X and Y , G and Y may stay adjacent in the skeleton due to collider bias, if the association through the path G → X ← U → Y is large enough in magnitude to be significant in the conditional independence test. Our rules will produce false-negative errors in this situation, removing potentially valid instruments. In summary, this shows that by inspecting the learned skeleton, one can select variables for which the above-stated MR assumptions hold, assuming no latent confounding. However, the selection may be flawed if not all relevant variables are measured. We investigate to what extent confounding impacts the performance of our algorithm in extensive simulation experiments below.

Our procedure to learn the skeleton is based on a GPU-accelerated version of the PC-stable algorithm 21 , 24 , which we additionally accelerated by iterative variable selection and by exploiting the LD-block structure of the genome. This enables us to construct a complete marker-trait graph, for millions of markers and tens of traits, despite the exponential run-time scaling in the number of variables of the PC algorithm. One challenge here is that the PC algorithm relies on partial correlations vanishing for (conditionally) independent variables, which generally holds for Gaussian variables? but not necessarily for binary or ordinal variables. We find that treating binary case-control outcomes like Gaussian variables can lead to largely elevated numbers of false positive findings, especially for independence tests between markers with very low minor allele frequencies and binary traits with very unbalanced numbers of cases and controls (Supplementary Fig. 1 ). As has been shown in previous work 25 , a heterologous correlation matrix with Pearson correlations between Gaussian, polyserial between Gaussian and ordinal and polychoric correlations between ordinal variables can be used to prevent this issue. This effectively places binary variables on the liability scale and has the additional advantage of allowing comparisons among traits at the same scale, accounting for differences in outcome prevalence. At the sample size, lowest minor allele frequency and lowest trait prevalence in the UK Biobank data used in this study, using polyserial correlations between markers and case-control traits is effective in controlling the numbers of false positives (Supplementary Fig. 1 ).

This first step of the algorithm can be combined with the second to prioritize exposure-outcome pairs, through selection of risk factors that are most likely to have a significant directed partial correlation with a particular outcome. The second step is based on the RFCI algorithm 20 , which attempts to direct the edges of the learned skeleton, testing for the presence of latent confounding. We introduce a novel way to obtain order-independent separation sets that offer a conservative way of orienting trait relationships, that is, to learn which phenotypes have evidence for a potential directed relationship with each outcome. We also incorporate prior knowledge that markers precede traits temporally, which dramatically reduces computation time. We denote our version of RFCI as sRFCI. For further details, see Methods.

Taken together, we improve upon previously proposed graphical methods that were limited to few hundreds 26 or thousands 27 of genetic variables or relied on the construction of separate graphs for trait-trait and marker-trait relationships with pre-selected genetic variants by GWAS 17 . Combining graphical inference with standard MR methods takes advantage of the principled instrumental variable selection and the identification of relevant risk factors. This also advances previous work on graphical inference in MR 17 because now marker selection is made through joint estimation, where many variables can be conditioned on at once, and pleiotropic markers can be identified prior to MR inference, promising more accurate instrumental variable selection and improved MR performance as shown below.

CI-GWAS takes as input: (1) the matrix of marker-marker correlations (an LD matrix); (2) a matrix of marker-trait correlations; (3) a matrix of trait-trait correlations. This makes CI-GWAS applicable to summary-statistic data, since LD matrices, effect sizes of marker-trait associations, minor allele frequencies, trait variances and trait-trait correlations can be shared whilst preserving privacy.

Here, we study how the usage of IVs selected by CI-GWAS in MR compares to standard GWAS-based IV selection. To this end, we conduct a simulation study using 654,173 imputed genetic markers recorded on 458,747 UK Biobank individuals (see Methods). We generate strong unobserved confounding, U , influencing both the exposure and outcome of interest, and focus on the three MR assumptions, given above, by simulating six scenarios where: (1) genetic effects are strong and therefore easily identifiable and there is no horizontal pleiotropy, or latent genetic confounding (labeled: baseline, high power); (2) genetic effects are weak and therefore more difficult to identify, effects are estimated with higher error and there is no horizontal pleiotropy or latent genetic confounding (labeled: baseline, low power); (3) genetic effects are easily identifiable and there is latent genetic confounding (latent pleiotropy, high power); (4) genetic effects are difficult to identify and there is latent genetic confounding (latent pleiotropy, low power); (5) genetic effects are easily identifiable and there is both latent genetic confounding and horizontal pleiotropy (horizontal pleiotropy, high power), which is also termed correlated pleiotropy or heritable confounding in the literature; (6) genetic effects are difficult to identify and there is both latent genetic confounding and horizontal pleiotropy (horizontal pleiotropy, low power). For each scenario, we simulate the exposure to be either causal for the outcome with average causal effect A C E = 0.2, or non-causal for the outcome A C E = 0.0, resulting in 12 settings for which we simulate 100 replicates. Thus, we generate 1200 data sets in total, each with a sample size of 458,747 individuals and a feature size of 654,172 SNPs.

For each of these data sets, we select IVs in two ways. First, we run standard marginal linear regression for X and Y at each of the 654,172 SNPs and then select IVs as an independent set of SNPs (within 1Mb, with LD R 2 < 0.001) associated with X with p value ≤5 × 10 −8 , as is commonly done in MR studies. Second, we use CI-GWAS to select the IVs as described above: For a given exposure trait X and an outcome trait Y , any marker G , found to be adjacent to X and not adjacent to Y and for which all paths to Y contain X , is discovered as a valid instrument to test the effect of X on Y . We then use these IVs alongside their marginal GWAS regression coefficients in two commonly used MR approaches of inverse-variance weighting (IVW) and MR-Egger 12 to estimate the causal effect of the exposure X and outcome Y .

We find that selecting genetic IVs from CI-GWAS allows unbiased estimation of the ACE across all scenarios considered here, when using both IVW and MR-Egger, as shown Fig. 1b . This accurate ACE estimation is further reflected in the false positive rate (FPR) of zero for each of the twelve settings (Fig. 1c ). In contrast to that, we see a considerable effect of horizontal pleiotropy for both MR-methods used with GWAS selected IVs. Note here, FPR measures the proportion of simulation replicates where A C E = 0, but MR methods incorrectly identify a causal effect of the exposure X and outcome Y (at p -value ≤0.05/800), out of all actual negatives (100 replicates per setting where A C E = 0). While MR-Egger shows zero FPR and little bias in the baseline setting, this changes to clear bias and a FPR of 0.6 and close to 1 in the presence of horizontal pleiotropy. Similarly, bias and FPR increase markedly for IVW in that setting. This suggests that the usage of IVs selected by CI-GWAS can help to avoid biases and false positives in MR inference that are introduced through either latent or horizontal pleiotropy.

We then compare the IVs detected by CI-GWAS to those identified by the standard approach from GWAS summary statistics (associated with X with p -value ≤5 × 10 −8 with LD R 2 < 0.001 within 1Mb). True valid IVs are those that are simulated to be associated with X , but not pleiotropic with Y or U . We find that CI-GWAS has a true positive rate (TPR, defined as the proportion of IVs correctly identified) comparable to GWAS for the selection of valid IVs under the horizontal pleiotropy settings considered here, but with a slight loss of power (Fig. 1d ). Additionally, we calculate the proportion of selected IVs for X that are also causal for Y through a path that is not through X or pleiotropic with Y (labeled PHP: proportion of horizontally pleiotropic IVs in Fig. 1d ). We find that CI-GWAS selected IVs are less likely to be causal for Y through a path that is not through X or pleiotropic with Y than IVs selected through GWAS, which explains why CI-GWAS improves causal effect estimates under both latent and horizontal pleiotropy.

As mentioned above, the graphical model learned by CI-GWAS indicates which potential causal relationships are compatible with the data's conditional independence structure. Consequently, one can use it to filter out hypothetical causal relationships that are not compatible with that conditional independence structure, with the aim of reducing the number of false positive results and exploring the nature of the trait relationships. Here, we explore two ways of doing that: (1) we inspect the skeleton and filter for pairs of variables that are adjacent. While non-adjacent pairs of variables may generally be in a causal relationship with each other, that relationship is mediated at least by one other observed variable, and the effect is therefore not direct. (2) We inspect the PAG and filter for pairs between which there is a directed or semi-directed edge, as for these, the conditional independence structure of the data does not provide any evidence against the existence of a causal effect (see Methods for more details).

We conduct an additional simulation experiment to investigate the effect of these filters. For that, we repeat the data generation for the four horizontal pleiotropy scenarios described above (high/low power and ACE=0.0/ACE=0.2 for X 1 to Y ), but modified the graph to include an additional exposure variable ( X 2), which does not have a causal effect on Y (ACE=0.0 for X 2 to Y , see Fig. 2 a and Methods). Thus, here, true causal relationships exist only from X 1 onto Y , and horizontal pleiotropy occurs either through unmeasured variables or through X 2. To perform the MR tests, we use IVW and multivariable inverse-variance weighting (MVIVW). We then assess the performance with and without the above described filtering strategies, which yields three distinct scenarios: MR tests are run on all exposure-outcome pairs (labeled s1 in Fig. 2 ); MR tests are run only on exposure-outcome pairs that are adjacent in the skeleton (labeled s2); and lastly, MR tests are run only on exposure outcome pairs for which there is either a directed or semi-directed edge from exposure to outcome in the PAG (labeled s3). For edges that were filtered out, we set the inferred A C E = 0 for the calculation of the performance metrics. We then calculate the FPR, TPR and true discovery rate (TDR) of the inferred causal relationships, where we calculate the rates as proportions of simulation replicates, since in each replicate, there is at most one causal link between an exposure and the outcome. For example, the FPR measures the proportion of simulation replicates where the true A C E = 0, but we incorrectly identify a causal effect of one of the exposures, X 1 or X 2, on the outcome Y . We find that the proposed filters are effective in reducing the FPR when using GWAS-selected IVs, but have only a little room left to reduce the FPR when using CI-GWAS selected IVs (Fig. 2b ), since that in itself brings the FPR down to almost 0, as already shown above (Fig. 1c ). Analyzing the effect on the TPR (Fig. 2b ), we see that the filters are not perfectly specific to false positives, but remove true positives as well, showing a classical recall-precision tradeoff, which is already evident when focusing only on the effect of GWAS vs CI-GWAS selected markers (s1). This is because, particularly in low-powered settings, the causal relationship between X1 and Y cannot always be directed due to simulated unobserved confounding and horizontal pleiotropy. Looking at the TDR, i.e., the proportion of identified causal effects that are actually true, we see that CI-GWAS-selected IVs yield extremely precise results across all settings with TDRs at or above 0.85. When looking only at relationships that can be directed, the TDR is further improved with the filters up to a TDR close to 1, even in the low power scenario. When using GWAS-selected IVs, we see that the PAG filter (s3) can bring a strong TDR improvement of about 0.2. The effects of the filters on the performance are consistent across IVW and MVIVW, with MVIVW generally yielding higher TDR at similar TPR, compared to IVW. Overall, we see that by trading recall for precision, CI-GWAS provides ways to refine causal inference in these simulation settings.

In the settings above, we have explored CI-GWAS in a very classical setting where it is pre-determined which traits are potential exposures and which are outcomes. Here, we move to a more complex scenario where we have a set of traits of interests and make no such assumptions about the causal structure, but instead allow that every trait might be causal for any other trait. Starting there, our aim is to infer the structure of the causal graph that relates these traits.

To study how well such a task can be solved by using CI-GWAS in conjunction with MR, we create an expanded simulation study in which we simulate many correlated traits and multiple latent confounders. We use a structural equation model consisting of twelve continuous traits, two of which are latent confounders and are not used in the inference. Each trait is influenced by a set of 50 causal markers randomly selected from 654,173 imputed genetic markers recorded for 458,747 UK Biobank individuals. Here, we include two additional MR approaches in the comparison, namely CAUSE 11 and MV-PRESSO 8 , in addition to MVIVW. We compare their performance when used with GWAS IV selection (MR ( I V G )) as input, and in conjunction with CI-GWAS IVs (MR ( I V C I G )). We then repeat the analyses using the CI-GWAS filters of the learned adjacencies (+ adj: using all adjacent pairs in the skeleton) or the PAG (using all pairs with evidence of a directed relationship). Since we assume that there are no pre-determined exposures and outcomes, we run CAUSE, which is a single-outcome, single-exposure model, for each simulated trait pair. For the multivariable approaches, we test each trait as an outcome, with all other traits treated as risk factors. When using the CI-GWAS inferred graph as a filter: we only conduct MR testing with CAUSE for trait pairs that have an adjacency, or a corresponding directed edge in the PAG; while for the multivariable approaches, we only select traits to include as exposures that have an adjacency, or a corresponding directed edge in the PAG. We simulate only a well-powered setting with a limited degree of horizontal pleiotropy as this allows us to compare approaches in an idealistic setting, where the results are not obscured by the lack of implicit control for horizontal pleiotropy of GWAS IV selection (see Methods). We run 20 replicates as this number was sufficient to support the conclusions of the simulations that we have already presented above.

We make the following observations: First, as shown above in Fig. 2 , filtering standard MR results with the CI-GWAS-learned adjacencies increases the TDR for all three tested MR methods (MR ( I V G ) vs. MR ( I V G ) + adj in Fig. 3 ). Second, the TDR is further increased, at the expense of power (TPR), by using the PAG instead of the skeleton for filtering (MR ( I V G ) + adj vs. MR ( I V G ) + PAG in Fig. 3 ). Third, for methods such as MV-PRESSO and MVIVW, only by using the PAG for filtering is an FDR of 0.05 achieved at a p -value threshold of 0.05 for the testing of the average causal effect (Fig. 3b ). Fourth, as CAUSE conducts variable selection on the marginal GWAS associations to select IVs, we find no evidence for improved performance when restricting CAUSE to using only CI-GWAS selected IVs. However, inference is more precise, with higher power when using the CI-GWAS-learned adjacencies. Finally, MVIVW with the PAG learned by CI-GWAS and CI-GWAS-selected IVs has a comparable FDR of 0.05 to CAUSE, but has significantly improved TPR. We find that these results remain largely consistent with different selection thresholds for GWAS (p-value ≤10 −4 ), when more markers are selected (Supplementary Figs. 2, 3, 5 ) and when pleiotropic effects are removed from the simulation (Supplementary Figs. 3, 5 ). Thus, we show that learning a graphical model, as in CI-GWAS, can be used in conjunction with traditional MR methods to improve precision.
